Base case unchanged (probabilities retuned) · Not investment advice

Not yet a confirmed bottom. Friday’s early close was a broad rally: all eleven Select Sector SPDRs finished higher, the S&P, Dow and Nasdaq all rose, and the VIX closed at 23.81, leaving the 25–35 mid-range but not yet back below 20. The S&P and the Dow remain outside a formal correction, but the S&P and the Nasdaq Composite have still not recaptured their 5 November closing lows. The base case remains a choppy extension—a single thin early-close bounce is not confirmation of a bottom (Monday’s bounce later faded as well).

The S&P 500’s official Friday early close was 7,297.49 (+1.60%, +114.71 points), session 7,304.10／7,211.46, open 7,262.61, −6.67% from the 6 October closing high of 7,818.93, still outside a formal correction (usually measured as −10% from a closing high) and tighter than Wednesday’s −8.14%. The Dow was 50,774.94 (+1.18%, +591.99 points), session 50,830.19／50,398.29, open 50,458.86, −6.58% from its high, still outside a correction and up for a fourth straight session. The Nasdaq Composite was 24,129.50 (+2.31%, +543.70 points), high 24,149.09, low 23,690.60, open 23,958.46, −12.57% from its high, still in a formal correction, YTD +3.82%. The VIX closed at 23.81 (−4.48 points / −15.84% versus Wednesday’s official 28.29), out of the 25–35 mid-range but still above 20; open 24.89, high 27.52, low 23.81 (Cboe official history, Friday close 23.81; Cboe/CNBC also list a Thanksgiving official close of 26.80, and print the day change as −2.99 / −11.16%). This episode’s intraday high of 40.03 on 20 November remains the first touch of 40; the VIX has still never closed at or above 40. The Nasdaq-100 closed at 26,726.39 (+2.61%, +679.49 points; high 26,757.20, low 26,166.87, open 26,479.97), −14.41% from its high, and has recaptured its 5 November close. SOX rose +4.69% (9,186.71, +411.84 points), to −37.23% from its high, also above its 5 November close. NVDA closed at 150.49 (+0.80%; Reuters noted it was weak for most of the session before finishing higher). The Russell 2000 closed at 2,750.30 (+1.71%, +46.24 points), −10.37% from its high, up for a fourth session and back above its 5 November close. The S&P at 7,297.49 is still below the 5 November closing low of 7,353.73, and the Nasdaq Composite at 24,129.50 is still below that day’s close of 24,315.00. For the week (versus the 20 November close) the S&P was +5.60%, the Nasdaq +6.68% and the Dow +5.46%. The official 10-year Treasury cash yield on 27 November was 4.94% (9 bp above 4.85% on the 25th; the 2-year was 4.69%, 8 bp above 4.61% on the 25th). The latest official HY OAS is 377 bps (3.77% on 26 November, the same as the 25th, updated on FRED on 27 November; the 27 November official print is still unpublished, with the next release dated 30 November). Official October CPI/PPI/payrolls and the BEA 25 November GDP second estimate and October PCE are unchanged. ChartRow as of the Friday early close, 27 November: S&P shares above the 50- / 200-day averages were 64% / 60% (317／499, 297／497), with 55% above the 20-day; advancers / decliners were 405／94 (81% up, 1 unchanged); new highs / new lows 23／0. The share of names ≥10% / ≥20% below the 52-week high was 62% / 35% (312／174 of 500). Nasdaq-100 / Composite moving-average breadth was not updated on ChartRow for Friday; the 11 November figures of 54.0%／53.5% and “50.0% ≥20% below the high” remain labelled as of that date and are not interpolated. Friday was a broad but thin post-Thanksgiving 13:00 ET early close; the VIX has never confirmed panic at a close, official credit is still far from a crisis zone, 200-day breadth is far above a washout, and the S&P and Nasdaq Composite have not recaptured their 5 November closing lows, so C is not raised to the base case and a single early-close bounce is not treated as a confirmed bottom. Probabilities: B 50% / A 12–18% / C 32–38%.

This update

Wednesday’s steep drop was largely recouped; the close was mixed

Friday’s early close was a broad rally: the S&P closed at 7,297.49 (+1.60%, +114.71 points), the Nasdaq Composite at 24,129.50 (+2.31%), the Nasdaq-100 at 26,726.39 (+2.61%), and the PHLX Semiconductor index at 9,186.71 (+4.69%), with the SOX distance from its ATH narrowing to −37.23%. NVDA closed at 150.49 (+0.80%; Reuters noted it was weak for most of the session before finishing higher). The Dow at 50,774.94 (+1.18%) and the Russell 2000 at 2,750.30 (+1.71%) rose again, each up for a fourth session. All eleven Select Sector SPDRs finished higher: Technology (XLK +2.80%) led, followed by Consumer Discretionary (XLY +2.11%) and Communication Services (XLC +1.99%); the laggards, still higher, were Utilities (XLU +0.28%) and Health Care (XLV +0.28%). Consumer Staples (XLP) closed at 92.68, a new closing high. All 11 sector funds rose and three fell. This dashboard uses only official cash closes that have been cross-checked.

The S&P and the Dow remain outside a formal correction; the Nasdaq is deeper in one

The S&P is −6.67% from the 6 October closing ATH (7,818.93), tighter than Wednesday’s −8.14%, and still outside a formal 10% correction. The Dow is −6.58% from its high (Yahoo daily ATH 54,349.12, 5 August), still outside a correction and up for a fourth session. The Nasdaq −12.57%, NDX −14.41% and QQQ −14.31% remain in a correction. SOX has narrowed to −37.23% from its ATH. Equal-weight RSP is −2.22% from its high, still shallower than cap-weighted SPY at −6.52%. QQEW is −14.72% from its high. The S&P and the Nasdaq Composite have not recaptured the 5 November closing lows (7,353.73 / 24,315.00); the NDX, SOX and Russell have recaptured those closes.

VIX closed at 23.81, out of the mid-range correction band

Down 4.48 points (−15.84%) from Wednesday’s official 28.29. The session opened at 24.89, with a high of 27.52 and a low of 23.81 (Cboe official history, Friday close 23.81; Cboe/CNBC also list a Thanksgiving official close of 26.80, and print the day change as −2.99 / −11.16%). Close path …→25.46→24.56→28.44→35.89→26.62→26.36→28.29→28.29. Last Friday’s intraday high of 40.03 remains this episode’s first touch of 40, but it has never closed at or above 40—the “VIX ≥ 40” item on the checklist is still counted on a close. The unusually wide Monday range with a Yahoo / Pivox intraday low of 15.39 still awaits official Cboe history.

Breadth broadened; all eleven sectors finished higher

ChartRow as of the Friday early close, 27 November: S&P shares above the 50- / 200-day averages were 64% / 60% (317／499, 297／497), still far above the <20% washout zone; 55% were above the 20-day. Advancers / decliners were 405／94 (81% up, 1 unchanged), and new highs / new lows were 23／0. The share of names ≥10% / ≥20% below the 52-week high was 62% / 35% (312／174 of 500), an improvement from Wednesday’s 64% / 38%. All eleven sector funds finished higher—a broadly participated bounce, not a cap-weighted-only rally. Nasdaq-100 / Composite moving-average breadth was not updated on ChartRow for Friday; the 11 November figures of 54.0%／53.5% and “50.0% ≥20% below the high” are still labelled as of that date and are not interpolated. Official raw NYSE advance / decline counts could not be independently verified, so they are not invented.

BEA published the GDP second estimate and October PCE; CPI / payrolls are unchanged; the 10-year is 4.94%; the latest official credit print is 377 bps (26 Nov)

The Bureau of Economic Analysis released at 8:30 ET on 25 November: third-quarter 2026 real GDP, second estimate, +4.3% SAAR (advance +3.4%, revised up 0.9 percentage point; Q2 +2.2%), and +2.3% year on year (percent change from the same quarter a year earlier, BEA / FRED). October headline PCE prices were +0.3% MoM and +3.8% YoY; core PCE was +0.3% MoM and +3.3% YoY (the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge). October payrolls +165k, U-3 4.1%, CPI MoM above forecast and PPI YoY +6.5% still have no new official print; October CPI YoY remains unpublished (next scheduled: payrolls 4 December, CPI 10 December, PPI 15 December; the GDP third estimate and November PCE are both 23 December, 8:30 ET / 21:30 HKT). The official 10-year cash yield on 25 November was 4.85% (Treasury; 6 bp below 4.91% on the 24th), still below 5%; the 2-year was 4.61% (2 bp below 4.63% on the 24th). Yahoo ^TNX was about 4.848 on Wednesday, consistent with the official print. The latest official HY OAS is 372 bps (24 November 3.72%, updated by FRED at 9:13 AM CST on the 25th, 9 bps wider than 363 bps on the 23rd); as of Friday morning in Hong Kong, the 25 and 26 November official prints are still unpublished (26 November was Thanksgiving, so the US credit market was closed and no print is expected). The judgment that the labour market has not broken and that inflation remains sticky is unchanged.

The framework is not overturned; the base case remains continued volatility

Friday’s early-close rally was broad and still did not confirm a bottom. The S&P and the Dow remain outside a formal correction at the close, with narrower drawdowns; the Nasdaq is still in a correction, and SOX is −37.23% from its ATH. Near-bottom probabilities stay at 10–16% and the bear-market-extension tail stays at 34–40%; base case B remains 50%. C is not raised to the base case, and this is not a confirmed panic bottom: the 5 November closing lows have not been recaptured, the VIX closed at 23.81, out of the mid-range but still above 20, and has never closed ≥40, the latest official HY OAS of 377 bps is still far below 450–600, and 200-day breadth at 60% is far above a washout. The closer analogies remain early/late 2018, 2015–16, and early-2022 theme weakness, not a 2020 or April 2025 shock bottom. Thursday 26 November was Thanksgiving, and the US cash equity market was closed; Friday is a 13:00 ET early-close session that had not opened at this Hong Kong morning compile. USD/JPY’s Yahoo Wednesday close was 159.262; offshore renminbi (USD/CNH) was about 6.6642 in Friday morning trade (Yahoo, about 10:49 HKT, not an official settlement).

COMEX December gold’s official Friday settlement was 3,639.60 (up 103.80 / 2.94% from Wednesday’s official 3,535.80; Dow Jones Data Talk); silver was 43.167 (up 3.109 / 7.76% from Wednesday’s official 40.058; Dow Jones Data Talk). Both remain well below their January highs. Gold and silver are moving with risk appetite and are not enough to read as a panic bid for haven assets.

Yen: not a classic haven rally

The intraday high on 13 November had reached 160.18; Yahoo’s Friday close was 159.281 (CNBC 159.55 at 16:59 ET — the two disagree), so this page uses the Yahoo daily close and flags the disagreement. In a typical risk-off move the yen often strengthens (USD/JPY falls). The current tape is still not fully consistent with a strong “haven yen” path.

Dollar: Friday official close slightly firmer

The official Friday cash DXY close was 104.04 (CNBC 104.035, about 0.36% above Wednesday 103.665 / 103.67; Yahoo daily 104.014, a slight disagreement). The official 10-year is 4.94%. The dollar still looks like rate- / differential-driven range trading at a high level, not a single equity-crash panic signal.

Reading versus equities / a risk-off shutdown: Cross-assets still look more like “yields still relatively high, official Friday oil settlements down versus their latest prior official prints, and official gold and silver settlements up rather than a panic bid.” USD/JPY’s Yahoo Friday close was 159.281; offshore renminbi (USD/CNH) closed at 6.6542 in the Friday FX session — moves in a rate- / differential-driven setting, not a US cash-equity close signal. That is consistent with this report’s base case of continued volatility without a confirmed panic-bottom package, and it does not rewrite the equity or breadth facts. Reading against the market framework (this is not investment advice)
BEA on 25 November published a Q3 GDP second estimate of +4.3% (revised up) and October PCE of +3.8% YoY / core +3.3%; official BLS October CPI / PPI / NFP are unchanged. The data support “growth has not collapsed, sticky inflation, a labor market that has not yet weakened, continued volatility, no panic bottom yet seen”—macro does not overturn the framework; scenario probabilities on the equity side are in Overview and Bottoming judgment.

October headline PCE was +0.3% MoM and +3.8% YoY, and core PCE was +0.3% MoM and +3.3% YoY (BEA, 25 November); the Q3 real GDP second estimate was +4.3% SAAR, revised up from the advance. October CPI MoM came in above forecast, and the core has been stuck at +0.3% for a third straight month (official YoY is still unpublished); PPI MoM slowed, but the YoY of 6.5% is about a four-year high; payrolls and the revisions remain relatively strong. Inflation looks sticky, with some signs of re-acceleration, the labor market has not weakened, and growth has not collapsed. That supports, rather than rewrites, the existing framework, and is not a labor-market break or a fully risk-off close. At Monday's equity close the S&P and the Dow were already back out of a formal correction, and the Nasdaq turned positive year-to-date; scenario probabilities are tweaked again to: B continued volatility 50%／A near a bottom 10–16%／C a bear market 34–40%. Monday's official settlements on the cross-asset page—still-soft oil, gold and silver rising with risk appetite, DXY about 104.33, and the official 10-year still at 4.92%—sit alongside this macro picture. The immediate force of the rates catalyst has eased somewhat, and does not rewrite the framework.

Closest analogues and non-analogues (one line per event)

Volmageddon 2018

−10.1%, only about 13 days to the low, but about 6 months to recover; VIX 50+ intraday. The current S&P −7.44% has already narrowed to shallower than that episode's final depth; this episode's intraday high remains 40.03 on 20 November, below that episode's 50+ intraday—if the path is similar, volatility could still last several months, and Monday's surge does not by itself end the analogy.

2015–16 grind

−14.2%, about 282 days to the low, more a “grind” than a “crash.” It remains the closest fit to the “continued volatility” base case—which can include both strong rebound sessions and stretches of macro softness.

Late 2018

ultimately −19.8%. If the current move is only a rebound after an opening leg, there is still room for the decline to deepen, but that would require credit and the labor market to deteriorate. Employment has not deteriorated so far; a renewed rise in yields bears watching, but is not by itself the same pressure as in that episode.

Early-2022 theme

Growth-stock / theme valuation compression came first, and later evolved into a full-year bear market. SOX is still −34.48% and NDX −14.34%, so that shadow remains (already narrower than Friday's −42.54%／−19.84%); whether it evolves depends on downward revisions to CapEx and earnings expectations.

Non-analogues: 2020 / 2025

COVID (−33.9%, VIX 82.69) and the 2025 tariff episode (−18.8%, VIX 60+ intraday) were shock-and-panic episodes; the signal mix is not the same as today's.

At more complete correction or bear-market lows since 2010, the share of the S&P above its 50-day average has often fallen to single digits or even close to 0%, and the share above the 200-day has commonly broken below 20%. Today those two figures are 59% and 55% (ChartRow, 25 November; 296／499, 273／497), up from Friday’s 43.1%／45.9% and from Monday’s 53%／53%, but still far above the <20% washout zone—there is no data support for calling today “already that kind of breadth washout bottom.”

Equal-weight S&P (RSP) gives each constituent a similar weight; cap-weighted (SPY) is led by the largest companies. “Who is falling” determines what breadth means. Figure 7 is still an earlier snapshot and has not been redrawn. Distances from highs: Monday SPY −7.29%, RSP −4.71%, QQQ −14.30%; official Tuesday SPY −7.74%, RSP −4.20%, QQQ −16.00%; official Wednesday SPY −8.01%, RSP −3.40%, QQQ −16.55%. Earlier dates are still listed alongside, and the already-verified figures are not used to invent precise 2020／2022 depths.

Bottoming judgment / scenarios

Probabilities are subjective approximate ranges within a historical framework, not the output of a forecasting model

At Friday’s early close the S&P and the Dow were still outside a formal correction, with narrower drawdowns; the tape was a broad rally and did not confirm a bottom. The Nasdaq remains in a correction and SOX is now −37.23% versus its ATH. The base case remains continued volatility (B). A single early-close bounce is not treated as confirmation of a bottom or of a new crash leg.

Breadth in one line
This episode still looks more like “continued volatility after a concentrated AI / cap-weighted-tech shakeout (with strong rebound sessions mixed in)” than like the 2011, late-2018, 2020, 2022 or April 2025 breadth washouts in which most stocks were washed below their moving averages together.

Broad-index drawdowns have narrowed from Friday's formal correction: the S&P −7.44% and the Dow −8.75% are both back out of correction territory; the Nasdaq −12.72% has turned back to ＋3.65% year-to-date. But the average stock (RSP −4.71%, 53% of the S&P above the 200-day) remains far from a washout, and the 5 November closing lows have not been recaptured. Levels continue to be revised; the framework has not flipped.

A｜Near a bottom

12–18%
Nudged in this edition from 12–18%

Friday’s early-close rally was broad, so the near-bottom probability is nudged up from 10–16% to 12–18%. The conditions are still not in place: the S&P and the Nasdaq Composite have not recaptured the 5 November closing lows. A single thin early-close bounce is not confirmation of a bottom (Monday’s bounce later faded as well). The 5 November closing lows have not been recaptured, and a single tech-led session followed by a giveback is not enough to count as a “broadening repair.”

Still need to see: a repair that is sustained, not a single session, and not confined to the technology sector, and that can re-establish itself above the 5 November closing lows. VIX closed at 23.81, out of the mid-range but still above 20; the typical panic washout of “first close above 40, then fall back” has still not appeared. The latest official HY OAS of 377 bps (26 November) also remains far from the crisis zone.

32–38%

A drawdown of −20%+; credit widening to 450–600 bps; a rising unemployment rate; theme-level cuts to capital expenditure.

Key observations:HY ≥ 450, a clear rise in U-3, and a collapse in corporate guidance. On Friday’s early close the S&P remains outside a correction with a narrower −6.67% drawdown, the NDX close −14.41%, SOX −37.23%, and VIX closed at 23.81, so this edition nudges C down from Wednesday’s 32–38% to 34–40%, without making C the base case. The latest official credit print of 372 bps (24 November) is far below 450 bps; VIX has never closed at or above 40, and the 54% share above the 200-day remains far above the washout zone, so C is not promoted to the base case, and Monday is not treated as a March 2020 or April 2025 shock bottom.

One-line conclusion · Not investment advice
Today looks more like “a surge that took the S&P and the Dow out of correction territory, without yet confirming a bottom,” not “a major bottom already confirmed.”

The base case remains continued volatility (a choppy extension). Friday’s early close was a broad rally, all eleven sectors finished higher, and the VIX closed at 23.81, leaving the mid-range; the S&P and the Dow remain outside a correction (−6.67% / −6.58%), the Nasdaq is still deeper (−12.57%), and shares above the 50- / 200-day averages were 64%／60%. Near-bottom probabilities are therefore nudged up from Wednesday’s 10–16% to 12–18%, and the bear-market-extension tail is nudged down from 34–40% to 32–38%, without promoting C to the base case or rewriting a single early-close bounce as a confirmed bottom. The 5 November closing lows have not been recaptured (S&P 7,353.73, Nasdaq 24,315.00); the latest official HY OAS of 376 bps remains well below 450–600; VIX has never closed at or above 40. A shift toward a near-bottom case would require a repair that is sustained, not a single session, and not confined to the technology sector—none of that set of conditions has appeared so far. Breadth that has not collapsed is not the same as an index that cannot fall further: because weights are highly concentrated, cap-weighted indexes can still correct further without a full breadth washout if earnings or CapEx expectations for AI / the mega-caps are revised down again. Cross-asset (the official 10-year still at 4.92%, DXY about 104.33 on Monday, gold and silver rising with risk appetite, official oil settlements still soft) looks closer to rate-driven chopping at high levels and a fading geopolitical premium than to panic hedging, and does not rewrite the framework above. As of 24 November (Hong Kong), the published official October CPI, PPI and payrolls prints are unchanged: inflation looks sticky, with some signs of re-acceleration, and the labor market has not weakened, which supports rather than rewrites the “continued volatility, no panic-bottom combination yet” framework. Today (Thursday 26 November) the cash market is closed for Thanksgiving; Friday has an early close at 13:00 ET.
